cards.title: Everything is built from atoms
cards.body: An atom is the smallest piece of an element that still acts like that element. Every atom has protons and neutrons packed in its center (the nucleus) with electrons zipping around them. Change the number of protons and you change the element itself.

cards.title: Protons decide identity
cards.body: Hydrogen has 1 proton. Helium has 2. Carbon has 6, oxygen has 8, gold has 79. The proton count — called the atomic number — is the element's ID card. Electrons decide how it behaves; neutrons mostly just add weight.
Remember the big three: protons = identity (who it is), electrons = personality (how it bonds), neutrons = luggage (adds mass, doesn't change the element).
Water is H₂O: two hydrogen atoms (1 proton each) plus one oxygen atom (8 protons). Same atoms, rearranged, give you hydrogen peroxide — H₂O₂ — which bleaches hair. Arrangement is everything.

cards.q: What decides which element an atom is?
cards.explain: Protons are the ID card. Change the proton count and you literally change the element — that's why it's called the atomic number.

flashcards.front: What are the three parts of an atom?
flashcards.back: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons orbiting around them.

flashcards.front: What does the atomic number tell you?
flashcards.back: The number of protons — which decides the element's identity.

flashcards.front: How many protons does carbon have?
flashcards.back: 6. That's what makes it carbon and not something else.
Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.q: Where are protons and neutrons found?
questions.explain: The nucleus is the dense center. Electrons are the ones flying around outside it.

questions.q: Hydrogen's atomic number is 1. That means...?
questions.explain: Atomic number = proton count, always. Hydrogen: 1 proton. Helium: 2. It's that direct.

choices: How an atom bonds with others
questions.explain: Electrons are the socialites — they form the bonds. Protons decide identity; neutrons add mass.

questions.q: Gold has 79 protons. An atom with 80 protons is...?
questions.explain: 80 protons = mercury, full stop. Proton count is identity; there's no negotiating with it.

questions.q: What does the ₂ in H₂O mean?
questions.explain: The subscript counts atoms of the element before it: H₂ means two hydrogens, O (no subscript) means one oxygen.

cards.title: Elements, organized by personality
cards.body: The periodic table lines up every known element by atomic number — but the magic is the columns. Elements in the same column (called groups) behave alike because they have the same number of outer electrons. It's a seating chart where neighbors share habits.

cards.title: Rows tell a story too
cards.body: Each row (called a period) adds a new electron shell. Sodium and magnesium sit side by side in row 3 — close in number, but sodium explodes in water while magnesium just fizzes. Position predicts personality.

Learn the famous neighborhoods: Group 1 (alkali metals) — violently reactive; Group 17 (halogens) — reactive the other way; Group 18 (noble gases) — refuse to react at all. Three groups cover most of chemistry's drama.
Table salt is NaCl — sodium (a metal that explodes in water) plus chlorine (a poisonous gas). Together? Harmless seasoning. The periodic table predicted they'd pair up: Group 1 loves Group 17.

cards.q: Why do elements in the same column behave alike?
choices: They have the same number of outer electrons
cards.explain: Outer electrons run the bonding show. Same count in the outer shell = same chemical habits, which is why the columns group them.

flashcards.front: What are the columns of the periodic table called?
flashcards.back: Groups — elements in a group behave alike.
Periods — each new row adds an electron shell.
Group 18, the noble gases (like helium and neon).

questions.q: Elements are ordered on the table by...?
questions.explain: It's strictly by proton count, left to right, top to bottom. Mendeleev's original had gaps where undiscovered elements belonged.

questions.q: Sodium (Na) and potassium (K) both fizz in water because...?
questions.explain: Both are Group 1 alkali metals with one outer electron to give away — same column, same explosive generosity.

choices: Their outer electron shell is full
questions.explain: A full outer shell means no reason to bond. Helium, neon, argon — content exactly as they are.

questions.q: What does the 'Cl' in NaCl stand for?
questions.explain: Cl is chlorine (Group 17). C is carbon, Ca is calcium — symbols aren't always obvious, which is why the table matters.

questions.q: Moving left to right across a period, atomic number...?
questions.explain: Each step right adds exactly one proton. That's the whole ordering principle of the table.

cards.title: Reactions are atom reshuffles
cards.body: In a chemical reaction, atoms break old bonds and form new ones — but no atom is created or destroyed. Burn wood and the carbon doesn't vanish; it joins oxygen and floats off as CO₂. Chemistry is rearrangement, not magic.

cards.title: Three classic moves
cards.body: Synthesis: two things join (hydrogen + oxygen → water). Decomposition: one thing splits (water → hydrogen + oxygen, with electricity). Combustion: something burns in oxygen, releasing heat and light. Most reactions you'll meet are one of these three.

Follow the energy: reactions that release heat (like burning) are exothermic — 'exo' means out. Reactions that absorb heat (like baking) are endothermic — 'endo' means in. The prefix tells you the direction.
Strike a match: wood + oxygen → CO₂ + water + heat + light. That's combustion — fast, hot, and bright. Your body does the same thing slowly with food: that's why eating keeps you warm.

cards.q: In a chemical reaction, atoms are...?
cards.explain: Conservation of mass: every atom you start with is still there at the end, just holding different hands.

flashcards.front: What happens to atoms in a reaction?
flashcards.back: They're rearranged into new substances — never created or destroyed.
Two or more substances joining into one (hydrogen + oxygen → water).
Burning in oxygen — releases heat and light.
Exothermic releases heat (burning); endothermic absorbs it (baking).

questions.q: Burning wood produces CO₂ and water. The carbon...?
choices: Joined oxygen and floated off as CO₂
questions.explain: Atoms don't vanish — the wood's carbon bonded with oxygen. Heat and light are energy released, not matter destroyed.

questions.q: Hydrogen + oxygen → water is an example of...?
questions.explain: Two substances joining into one is synthesis. Splitting apart would be decomposition.

questions.q: Using electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen is...?
questions.explain: One compound breaking into simpler pieces is decomposition — the reverse of synthesis.

questions.q: Why does eating keep you warm?
choices: Your body slowly 'burns' food with oxygen
questions.explain: Cellular respiration is slow combustion: food + oxygen → CO₂ + water + energy. Same chemistry as fire, just controlled.
Endo = in. Baking, melting ice, photosynthesis — all pull heat in. Exothermic pushes it out.
